title: The permitting deal is good and should pass
gist: Yglesias backs the 2026 federal permitting reform bill. It eases NEPA review for transmission and clean energy, and also for natural-gas pipelines. He argues that blocking gas infrastructure, as New England has done, raises power prices and oil use without producing clean energy. He calls US oil and gas exports a geopolitical asset against Russia, and says green absolutism undercuts Democrats' big-tent coalition.

insights.claim: The new 2026 permitting reform bill would speed clean-energy deployment, but many of its changes, including NEPA exemptions, also apply to replacing, upgrading, expanding or extending existing natural-gas pipelines and compressor stations.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Passage would lower project risk and timelines for both transmission developers and gas midstream operators.

insights.claim: Yglesias reports that green groups said on an internal strategy call that they would publicly claim to be improving the permitting bill while actually working to kill it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Organized environmental opposition is a real risk to the bill's passage.
insights.quote: green groups explained on their internal strategy call that the plan is to say they’re pushing to improve the bill while actually working to kill it.

insights.claim: Treating permitting reform as climate policy is a bet that battery storage keeps getting cheaper and better, rather than hitting a wall once the summer market is saturated.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Battery cost curves are the key variable deciding whether easier permitting yields decarbonization; this favors storage names.
insights.quote: It’s a bet that the battery optimists are correct that storage technology will keep getting better and cheaper

insights.claim: The permitting bet also assumes future Democratic administrations can pass substantive air-pollution rules instead of relying on procedural obstacles to hobble fossil-fuel infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shifts regulatory risk for fossil assets from permitting to emissions rules.

insights.claim: Solar made up 11.3% of US electricity in July 2026, up from 9.5% a year earlier, and a record 9.5% over the trailing twelve months.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Solar share keeps compounding; it supports demand for grid, storage and transmission buildout.
insights.quote: Solar power made up 11.3% of US electricity this July, up from 9.5% last year

insights.claim: Yglesias calls the strategy of blocking new natural-gas infrastructure to reach net zero 'underpants gnome' climate policy: it has no workable technical or political mechanism.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Suggests pipeline-blocking will keep failing to deliver decarbonization, so the political case for permitting deals grows.
insights.quote: It’s just not clear how this is supposed to work technically or politically.

insights.claim: The northeastern US lacks enough pipelines to meet New England's gas demand, so the region imports LNG, which trades on global markets above pipeline gas prices.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: New England power and heating costs are tied to global LNG prices, raising regional energy-price volatility.
insights.quote: As a result, the region imports liquefied natural gas (L.N.G.), which trades on global markets at a higher price than pipeline gas.

insights.claim: Renewables deployment depends more on physical fundamentals — wind, sun, land prices and land access — than on a state's politics, which is why the Great Plains lead in wind and the Southwest in solar.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Renewable buildout and its investment returns will concentrate where resources and cheap land are, not in progressive states.
insights.quote: In the real world, renewables deployment has less to do with the ideological complexion of states and more to do with the physical fundamentals.

insights.claim: Texas has become a solar champion partly because it has many large parcels of privately owned, low-value agricultural land.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Land availability is a structural edge for Texas utility-scale solar development.
insights.quote: One reason Texas has become such an extraordinary solar champion is that Texas features many large parcels of privately owned low-value agricultural land.

insights.claim: New England is less sunny, less windy, more expensive, more forested and has more fragmented land ownership, so utility-scale renewables there would need affirmative policy such as eminent domain to assemble land.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Limits renewable supply growth in New England, so high regional power prices persist.

insights.claim: Blocking gas infrastructure in New England leads power stations to burn dirtier oil during adverse weather and keeps regional electricity relatively expensive.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Winter oil-burn and price spikes are recurring features of the New England power market.

insights.claim: In New York Times state-by-state data, Washington and Oregon offer the best EV-versus-gasoline savings, while the five worst states are all progressive Northeastern states with expensive electricity.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: High power prices suppress EV adoption in the Northeast, which matters for regional EV and charging demand.
insights.quote: But the five worst states are all politically progressive states in the Northeast, where electricity is expensive.

insights.claim: Expensive New England electricity makes heat pumps less attractive, and more heat-pump adoption without new generation would push prices even higher.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Electrification demand is limited by supply; generation buildout is the bottleneck for heat-pump and EV markets.

insights.claim: Yglesias argues a permitting deal actually increases clean electricity, while expanded gas infrastructure has an ambiguous environmental effect and pure pipeline blocking is clearly failing.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Frames permitting reform as net-positive for clean-energy supply growth.
insights.quote: A permitting deal, by contrast, actually does increase the amount of clean electricity.

insights.claim: A law that makes both gas and renewable infrastructure easier to build clearly improves affordability and the cost of living, unlike the disputed climate impact.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Affordability framing could win over swing-vote Democrats, raising the bill's chances of passing.
insights.quote: You have disagreements over impact within the climate camp, but the cost-of-living impact is unambiguous.

insights.claim: Bill McKibben compares the permitting deal to the 2015 deal that paired clean-energy tax credits with lifting the crude-oil export ban, which he calls disastrous because it made America the world's largest hydrocarbon exporter.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows the main left-wing objection: any gain for oil and gas counts as a climate loss.
insights.quote: Over the course of a decade they turned America into the world’s largest hydrocarbon exporter, and rewrote the shape of global energy markets.

insights.claim: Yglesias argues that without the 2015 deal, repeal of the oil export ban would probably have passed in 2017 anyway, while Democrats from oil-and-gas states would have taken the political hit for filibustering it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Pro-production energy policy is durable across administrations.
insights.quote: In the real world, a repeal of the export ban would probably just have passed in 2017.

insights.claim: A potential 2026 Democratic Senate majority hinges on seats in Alaska and Texas, creating a tradeoff between building a big-tent anti-MAGA coalition and fighting the fossil-fuel industry.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Democrats who need energy-state seats are likely to soften anti-fossil positions.
insights.quote: Here in the real world, we’re looking at a potential Democratic Senate win that hinges on seats in Alaska and Texas.

insights.claim: Without US oil and gas exports over the past decade, sanctioning Russia would have been impossible and Europe would be entirely dependent on Putin's energy.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: US LNG exports are a strategic asset that supports long-term policy support for export capacity.
insights.quote: Sanctioning Russia would be impossible and unthinkable.

insights.claim: Europe has been investing in renewables while relying on American fossil-fuel exports as a bridge.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: European demand for US LNG is structural through the energy transition.

insights.claim: Yglesias argues that trying to curb global fossil-fuel use by restricting American production has a terrible cost-benefit profile and always will.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Supply-side restrictions on US production are unlikely to cut global consumption; they shift market share abroad.
insights.quote: Efforts to influence global fossil-fuel consumption by constraining American fossil-fuel production have a terrible cost-benefit profile and always will.

insights.claim: Yglesias says Trump's war in Iran has been destructive to the global economy, and likens green absolutists' goal of choking US fossil supply to Trump's disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Confirms ongoing Hormuz disruption as a live global energy-supply shock in 2026.
insights.quote: green absolutists want to do to the United States of America what Trump has done in the Strait of Hormuz.

insights.claim: The permitting compromise does not prevent a future Democratic administration from regulating fossil fuels under the Clean Air Act, or a Democratic trifecta from pricing carbon.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Long-dated regulatory risk for fossil assets remains even if the deal passes.

insights.claim: Yglesias floats a carbon price that might be limited to the deeply unpopular data-center industry.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers and AI data-center operators face a tail risk of targeted carbon pricing as they become politically unpopular.
insights.quote: perhaps one limited to the deeply unpopular data-center industry

insights.claim: Yglesias says the deal still leaves room to invest in technologies that cut fossil-fuel needs in aviation, maritime shipping, cement, steel and agriculture.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Hard-to-abate sectors remain a target for future decarbonization policy and capital.
